questions.q: Who was Isaiah?
questions.a: Isaiah was the son of Amoz.

questions.q: What was Isaiah’s vision about?
questions.a: Isaiah’s vision was about Judah and Jerusalem.

questions.q: When did Isaiah have his vision?
questions.a: Isaiah had his vision in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

questions.q: Why should the heavens hear and the earth listen?
questions.a: The heavens should hear and the earth should listen because Yahweh has spoken.

questions.q: What has Yahweh done?
questions.a: He has raised and brought up sons.

questions.q: What have Yahweh’s children done?
questions.a: They have rebelled against Yahweh.

questions.q: What do the ox and the donkey know that Israel does not know?
questions.a: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey knows where its master feeds it, but Israel does not know or understand Yahweh.

questions.q: How is the nation described?
questions.a: They are described as sinners, people full of iniquity, offspring of evildoers and sons that act corruptly.

questions.q: What has the nation done?
questions.a: They have forsaken Yahweh, despised the Holy One of Israel, and turned away from him.

questions.q: What are the people of Judah compared to because of their rebellion?
questions.a: They are compared to a person who has been beaten so badly that he can no longer think clearly and has lost all his courage.

questions.q: What does Isaiah compare the nation to?
questions.a: He compares the nation to a person whose whole body is covered with wounds, bruises, and open sores that no one has cleaned, treated with oil, or bandaged.

questions.q: What is the condition of their country and cities?
questions.a: Their country is desolate and their cities are burned.

questions.q: What is Jerusalem compared to in this verse?
questions.a: Jerusalem is compared to a shelter in a vineyard, a hut in a cucumber field, and a city under siege.

questions.q: What has Yahweh left them?
questions.a: He has left them a very small remnant.

questions.q: What does Isaiah tell the rulers and people of Judah to do?
questions.a: He tells them to hear the word of Yahweh and listen to the instruction of their God.

questions.q: What does not delight Yahweh?
questions.a: He does not delight in the blood of bulls, lambs, and male goats.

questions.q: What does Yahweh say he never asked them to do?
questions.a: He says he never asked them to trample his courts with their sacrifices.

questions.q: What does Yahweh tell them to stop doing?
questions.a: He tells them to stop bringing worthless offerings, because their incense disgusts him and he cannot endure their New Moon and Sabbath gatherings and their wickedness.

questions.q: What does Yahweh hate?
questions.a: He hates their new moons and annual festivals.

questions.q: Why will Yahweh not hear their prayers?
questions.a: He will not hear because their hands are full of blood.

questions.q: What does Yahweh tell them to do?
questions.a: Yahweh tells them to stop doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice, help those who are oppressed, defend the orphan, and plead for the widow.

questions.q: What does Yahweh say he will do with their sins?
questions.a: He says that even though their sins are like scarlet or crimson, he will make them white like snow or wool, meaning he will forgive them and make them clean.

questions.q: What must they do to eat the good of the land?
questions.a: They must be willing and obedient.

questions.q: What will happen if they refuse and rebel?
questions.a: The sword will devour them.

questions.q: What was Jerusalem like before it became like a prostitute?
questions.a: The people of Jerusalem used to treat each other fairly and do what was right.

questions.q: What did Jerusalem become full of?
questions.a: Jerusalem became full of murderers.

questions.q: What is used to describe how the people of Jerusalem have changed?
questions.a: They are described as silver that has become dross and wine that has been diluted with water, showing that they have become corrupt and weak.

questions.q: What does Isaiah say about the princes’ behavior?
questions.a: He says they are rebels and friends of thieves who love bribes and rewards, and they do not defend orphans or widows.

questions.q: What will Yahweh do?
questions.a: He will take vengeance against his adversaries.

questions.q: What will Yahweh do to purify the people?
questions.a: He will punish them and make them pure again, like a metalworker uses lye to remove impurities from silver.

questions.q: What will Yahweh restore?
questions.a: He will restore their judges and counselors as they were before, and the city will be called the City of Righteousness.

questions.q: How will Zion be redeemed?
questions.a: Zion will be redeemed with justice, and those who repent will be redeemed with righteousness.

questions.q: What will happen to transgressors, sinners, and those who forsake Yahweh?
questions.a: They will be destroyed together, and those who forsake Yahweh will come to an end.

questions.q: What will make them ashamed and embarrassed?
questions.a: They will be ashamed of the sacred oak trees they desired and embarrassed by the gardens they have chosen.

questions.q: What will the people be like?
questions.a: They will be like an oak tree with withering leaves or a garden that has no water.

questions.q: What will happen to the strong man and his work?
questions.a: They will both burn together.

commentary.text: The corruptions prevailing among the Jews. (Is. 1:1-9) Severe censures. (Is. 1:10-15) Exhortations to repentance. (Is. 1:16-20) The state of Judah is lamented; with gracious promises of the gospel times. (Is. 1:21-31)

Is. 1:1-9 Isaiah signifies, "The salvation of the Lord;" a very suitable name for this prophet, who prophesies so much of Jesus the Saviour, and his salvation. God's professing people did not know or consider that they owed their lives and comforts to God's fatherly care and kindness. How many are very careless in the affairs of their souls! Not considering what we do know in religion, does us as much harm, as ignorance of what we should know. The wickedness was universal. Here is a comparison taken from a sick and diseased body. The distemper threatens to be mortal. From the sole of the foot even to the head; from the meanest peasant to the greatest peer, there is no soundness, no good principle, no religion, for that is the health of the soul. Nothing but guilt and corruption; the sad effects of Adam's fall. This passage declares the total depravity of human nature. While sin remains unrepented, nothing is done toward healing these wounds, and preventing fatal effects. Jerusalem was exposed and unprotected, like the huts or sheds built up to guard ripening fruits. These are still to be seen in the East, where fruits form a large part of the summer food of the people. But the Lord had a small remnant of pious servants at Jerusalem. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed. The evil nature is in every one of us; only Jesus and his sanctifying Spirit can restore us to spiritual health.

Is. 1:10-15 Judea was desolate, and their cities burned. This awakened them to bring sacrifices and offerings, as if they would bribe God to remove the punishment, and give them leave to go on in their sin. Many who will readily part with their sacrifices, will not be persuaded to part with their sins. They relied on the mere form as a service deserving a reward. The most costly devotions of wicked people, without thorough reformation of heart and life, cannot be acceptable to God. He not only did not accept them, but he abhorred them. All this shows that sin is very hateful to God. If we allow ourselves in secret sin, or forbidden indulgences; if we reject the salvation of Christ, our very prayers will become abomination.

Is. 1:16-20 Not only feel sorrow for the sin committed, but break off the practice. We must be doing, not stand idle. We must be doing the good the Lord our God requires. It is plain that the sacrifices of the law could not atone, even for outward national crimes. But, blessed be God, there is a Fountain opened, in which sinners of every age and rank may be cleansed. Though our sins have been as scarlet and crimson, a deep dye, a double dye, first in the wool of original corruption, and afterwards in the many threads of actual transgression; though we have often dipped into sin, by many backslidings; yet pardoning mercy will take out the stain, Ps. 51:7. They should have all the happiness and comfort they could desire. Life and death, good and evil, are set before us. O Lord, incline all of us to live to thy glory.

Is. 1:21-31 Neither holy cities nor royal ones are faithful to their trust, if religion does not dwell in them. Dross may shine like silver, and the wine that is mixed with water may still have the colour of wine. Those have a great deal to answer for, who do not help the oppressed, but oppress them. Men may do much by outward restraints; but only God works effectually by the influences of his Spirit, as a Spirit of Judgment. Sin is the worst captivity, the worst slavery. The redemption of the spiritual Zion, by the righteousness and death of Christ, and by his powerful grace, most fully accord with what is here meant. Utter ruin is threatened. The Jews should become as a tree when blasted by heat; as a garden without water, which in those hot countries would soon be burned up. Thus shall they be that trust in idols, or in an arm of flesh. Even the strong man shall be as tow; not only soon broken, and pulled to pieces, but easily catching fire. When the sinner has made himself as tow and stubble, and God makes himself as a consuming fire, what can prevent the utter ruin of the sinner?
